catalog_quote: Takayama Michiaki (1981, 1982, 1983, 1984) has demonstrated statistical correlations between the Middle Japanese accent recorded in the Myôgishô (1081 CE) and the Middle Chinese tones of the phonograms of poems in the parts of Shoki which Mori (1991: 138) calls the 'alpha' section. The Chinese Level Tone corresponds to Japanese low pitch, and the Chinese 'oblique' tones (Rising, Departing, and Entering) correspond to Japanese high pitch ... From this evidence it would appear that OJ accent was not much different from that of Middle Japanese accent (Mori 1991: 138). ... Even within poems written with apparent accentual notation, there are mismatches between phonogram tones and the expected pitches of OJ syllables. ... audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding quotation (pp. 37-39, PDF 56-58) and the domain quotation (p. 25, PDF 44) are verbatim in the Miyake 2003 PDF we hold/txt at the stated locators. (2) Deciding source: a 2003 phonology monograph (phonetic reconstruction of OJ) that reviews the only primary evidence for OJ prosody — Takayama's Shoki phonogram-tone / Myogisho pitch correlation — and concludes OJ had a pitch accent close to EMJ's, explicitly with no reconstruction and no stress statement. For an extinct philological language this is the appropriate evidence base; Glottolog's higher-ranked grammars (Vovin 2005/2020 WOJ; Kupchik 2011/2023 EOJ) cannot rest on different evidence, and the downloaded Kupchik 2011 confirms EOJ accent is simply 'unknown' (silent, consistent with no-stress coding).

sources.quote: p. 3: 'The phonotactic structure is a strict (C)V, with no geminate consonants or long vowels. ... The accent system is unknown.' p. 677: 'There is no evidence such accentual differences were present in the EOJ dialects, since accent was not marked in the orthography.' No mention of stress anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: 'stress' occurs only in glosses 'distress').
